01 · Import and quality control of a DIA-NN plasma/serum report¶

Question: Can this data set be trusted, and what must normalization and statistics correct for later?

Input: a DIA-NN main report (precursor level) from PRIDE PXD018874: 209 SWATH runs of plasma, serum and a pooled QC. Outputs:

  • a filtered precursor table and a sample table with QC flags, saved to data/processed/ for Notebook 02
  • figures saved to figures/01_*.png

Approach: every QC metric answers a specific question. Each section states the question, computes the metric, and records the decision it leads to. Thresholds are set before looking at which runs they flag.

§ Question
1 Where does the data come from, and which decisions were made before it reached us?
2 What filters has the report already been through?
3 Can the run names give a reliable sample table, including injection order?
4 Do the columns mean what we think they mean?
5 Which identification filters should we add, and what does each cost?
6 Is identification depth stable across the run?
7 How much is missing, and why?
8 How precise is quantification?
9 Does signal drift with injection order?
10 Is retention time stable?
11 What drives variation between runs?
12 Does the data recover a known biological difference?
13 Which runs fail QC, and what is carried forward?

1. Data set and provenance¶

Source. Messner CB, Demichev V, Wendisch D, et al. Ultra-high-throughput clinical proteomics reveals classifiers of COVID-19 infection. Cell Systems 2020;11(1):11–24.e4. doi:10.1016/j.cels.2020.05.012. Data: PRIDE PXD018874.

Which experiment this is. These are the commercial plasma and serum control samples that were run alongside the paper's Generation Scotland (GS) serum study, not the COVID-19 cohort. The individual GS samples are under controlled access and are not in this file. From PRIDE and the STAR Methods:

  • commercial plasma and serum on four 96-well plates, prepared in parallel on a Biomek liquid handler
  • a pooled QC of commercial sera, spiked with iRT peptides, injected every 10th injection
  • reversed-phase LC at 800 µL/min, 3→36% B in 5 min, 50 mm C18 column, 5 µg injected
  • SCIEX TripleTOF 6600, SWATH with 25 variable windows over m/z 450–850
  • DIA-NN 1.7.10

How to use the authors' methods. Their methods tell us what was done upstream of this file, which we cannot change. They are not a template for what we do downstream. Each downstream step here is justified from this data; where we end up agreeing or disagreeing with the authors, the reason is shown.

Upstream decision (from the STAR Methods) What it means for this analysis Our response
DIA-NN 1.7.10 No global protein-group q-value and no peak-width output §5 builds a global protein filter from run-level q-values; §4 confirms there is no usable peak width. The authors measured peak width in different software (Spectronaut), consistent with that.
Public pan-human library, refined on this experiment at 1% global q The library contains only precursors DIA-NN found somewhere in this experiment (GS samples included), with spectra and RTs re-learned from it Identifications are experiment-specific, and a precursor may be present because it was found in the GS samples, not in these controls. §5 therefore requires repeated confident identification within these runs.
Report filtered at precursor q 0.01, library q 0.005, protein-group q 0.05 Confirms what §2 infers from the data alone §5 tightens the protein-group level
RT-dependent median normalisation enabled Precursor.Normalised is already drift-adjusted; Precursor.Quantity is raw QC uses raw quantities, because the normalised ones would hide the drift we need to measure (§9). DIA-NN's normalisation becomes one candidate in Notebook 02.
Protein quantities by MaxLFQ, computed outside DIA-NN The report's PG.Quantity is DIA-NN's internal value, not what the authors analysed §11 shows it cannot be reconstructed from the filtered precursors; protein-level results here are provisional. Notebook 02 rolls up precursors itself.
Drift corrected per precursor by a straight line vs injection number, using the QC Assumes the drift is linear §9 tests that assumption against this data.
iRT peptides spiked into the QC only The library is human-only, so iRT precursors are absent from the report iRT cannot be used for RT QC; §10 uses endogenous precursors.
Commercial pooled-donor materials: two serum and two plasma products are listed Each well holds pooled material, not one person. The file does not say which product went into which well. Analysed as unpaired groups. §8 tests whether wells within a matrix behave as replicates of one material.

2. Load the report and read its inherited filters¶

The report is about 350 MB. load_diann_report reads only the columns we use and caches a parquet copy, so later runs load in seconds. The maximum of each q-value column shows which FDR filter was applied before export.

Is this the same file? Before loading, confirm the download is byte-for-byte the file this notebook was built on.

  • A SHA-256 checksum is a fingerprint of the file's contents: change one byte and it changes completely.
  • If it does not match, every number below may differ. That is worth knowing before spending time on the analysis, not after.
In [2]:
import hashlib

# Read the file in 8 MB chunks so the whole 350 MB never has to sit in memory at once
sha = hashlib.sha256()
with open(RAW_REPORT, "rb") as fh:
    for chunk in iter(lambda: fh.read(8 * 1024 * 1024), b""):
        sha.update(chunk)

# Compare with the fingerprint recorded in the setup cell
if sha.hexdigest() == RAW_REPORT_SHA256:
    print("Checksum OK: this is the exact file the notebook was built on.")
else:
    print("WARNING: checksum differs from the analysed file.\n"
          f"  expected {RAW_REPORT_SHA256}\n  got      {sha.hexdigest()}\n"
          "  Results below may not match the published notebook.")

Checksum OK: this is the exact file the notebook was built on.

What this tells us

  • Precursors: already filtered at 1% FDR, both per run (Q.Value) and experiment-wide (Lib.Q.Value ≤ 0.5%).
  • Protein groups: filtered only at 5% per run (PG.Q.Value). About 30% of rows sit between 1% and 5% protein-group FDR. §5 decides what to do with them.
  • Protein.Q.Value reaches 1.0. It scores individual proteins in Protein.Ids, not the reported protein group, so it is not used for filtering.
  • Each precursor appears once per run, which describe_report confirms (0 duplicate precursor-run rows). Pivoting to a matrix will not silently average duplicates.

3. Build the sample table from run names¶

Run names follow the pattern Type_Plate-Well_Position_N, e.g. Plasma_1-F4_64_128. We read N as injection order. That reading is an inference, so it has to be tested before the drift analysis rests on it.

Evidence that N is injection order

  • N is unique for every run.
  • Pooled-QC runs fall exactly every 10 or 11 values. That matches the PRIDE description, "a pooled sample … injected every 10 injections."
  • §9 adds independent evidence: QC signal falls smoothly as N increases, which a random label would not produce.

Design

  • All four plates span the whole sequence, so plate is not confounded with run order. Drift and plate effects can be told apart. A design that ran plates one after another could not separate them.
  • N runs from 2 to 428, but only 209 runs are present. The STAR Methods explain the gaps: these controls were run within the Generation Scotland study (199 individual serum samples), and the individual-level runs are under controlled access. So the missing numbers are most likely those GS samples, plus any blanks. That matters for interpretation: the drift in §9 accumulated over about 428 injections of serum, not just over the 209 runs we see.

4. Check that the columns mean what we think they mean¶

Two quick checks, before any column is used as a QC metric.

In [8]:
width_s = (df["RT.Stop"] - df["RT.Start"]) * 60
print("Peak window RT.Stop - RT.Start (seconds):")
print(width_s.describe(percentiles=[0.01, 0.5, 0.99]).round(2).to_string())

quant = df["Precursor.Quantity"]
print(f"\nPrecursor.Quantity: {quant.isna().sum()} missing, {(quant <= 0).sum()} zero or negative values")

1%            4.44

99%           4.44

Precursor.Quantity: 0 missing, 0 zero or negative values

Findings

  • The peak window is the same width (4.44 s) for at least 98% of precursors. It is a fixed integration window written by DIA-NN, not a measured chromatographic peak width. So it cannot be used to track column performance, and peak width is left out of this QC. Plotting it would have produced a flat, reassuring line with nothing behind it.
  • Quantities are all positive and present. Missing values exist only as absent rows. They appear once the long table is pivoted into a matrix (§7).

5. Identification-confidence filters: what to add, and what each option costs¶

Precursors are already at 1% FDR. Protein groups are only at 5% per run. Protein q-values computed per run are a poor guide for low-abundance proteins: one run's call may rest on 1–2 precursors from a 5-minute gradient. Newer DIA-NN versions (1.8+) report a proper global protein-group q-value. This report does not, so we compare ways to approximate one.

Each rule is judged on two things:

  • how much depth it keeps
  • what happens to known plasma proteins:
    • fibrinogen (FGA, FGB, FGG): abundant in plasma, removed in serum by clotting. Any sensible rule must keep it.
    • VWF, F5, KNG1: genuine plasma proteins at lower abundance, used as a sensitivity probe. A strict rule is expected to lose some of them; the point is to see the cost explicitly.
In [9]:
support = qc.protein_group_support(df, meta, q=0.01)   # fraction of runs with PG q <= 1%, per sample type
best_q = df.groupby("Protein.Group")["PG.Q.Value"].min()
markers = ["FGA", "FGB", "FGG", "VWF", "F5", "KNG1"]

pg_rules = {
    "A  as delivered (PG q <= 5% per run)": lambda d: pd.Series(True, index=d.index),
    "B  PG q <= 1% per run": lambda d: d["PG.Q.Value"] <= 0.01,
    "C  PG q <= 1% in its single best run": lambda d: d["Protein.Group"].isin(best_q.index[best_q <= 0.01]),
    "D  PG q <= 1% in >= 25% of runs of one sample type": lambda d: d["Protein.Group"].isin(
        support.index[(support >= 0.25).any(axis=1)]),
    "E  PG q <= 1% in >= 50% of runs of one sample type": lambda d: d["Protein.Group"].isin(
        support.index[(support >= 0.50).any(axis=1)]),
}

rows = []
for name, rule in pg_rules.items():
    kept = df[rule(df)]
    per_run = kept.groupby("run", observed=True)
    genes_kept = set(kept["Genes"].dropna())
    rows.append({"rule": name,
                 # runs with ANY data left: a strict per-run rule can empty whole runs,
                 # and a median over the surviving runs would hide that
                 "runs with data": kept["run"].nunique(),
                 "protein groups": kept["Protein.Group"].nunique(),
                 "median PG / run": int(per_run["Protein.Group"].nunique().median()),
                 "median precursors / run": int(per_run["Precursor.Id"].nunique().median()),
                 **{g: "kept" if g in genes_kept else "LOST" for g in markers}})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("rule")

Decision: rule D. Keep a protein group if it reaches PG q ≤ 1% in at least 25% of the runs of at least one sample type. Then keep its precursors in every run where the inherited 5% filter passed.

Rule Why not
A Keeps protein groups whose only support is a 1–5% q-value. That FDR is 5x looser than the precursor level.
B Empties 42 of the 209 runs completely. With about 180 protein groups per run, the smallest q-value a run can produce is about 1/180 ≈ 0.006, and in 42 runs even the best protein misses 1%. In the surviving runs it halves the protein groups (278 → 139), so missingness is created by thresholding rather than by absence.
C Too permissive. Taking the best of 209 runs is a multiple-testing problem: with enough runs, a false protein clears 1% somewhere by chance.
E Removes 40 more protein groups than D and gains nothing on the probes.
  • D requires repeated confident identification within one matrix. It keeps fibrinogen, KNG1 and 180 protein groups per run.
  • The cost is VWF and F5. They pass 1% in at most 10% of the runs of any matrix, so in a 5-minute gradient they are at the edge of detection. Dropping them is the FDR filter working as intended (losing weakly supported true proteins), not a failure of it. If those two proteins mattered to a study, the fix would be a longer gradient, not a looser filter.
  • "Within one matrix" matters: fibrinogen is confidently identified in plasma but barely in serum, so a rule pooling all runs would penalise matrix-specific proteins.
  • Caveat: the 25% threshold is a judgment call, not an estimated FDR. If DIA-NN can be run later, a global protein q-value would replace this rule. Notebook 02 re-checks the key results under rules B and E.
  • Proteotypic peptides: Proteotypic = 0 marks a peptide shared between proteins. Those rows are kept and flagged here, because whether shared peptides count toward protein quantity is a roll-up decision for Notebook 02.
In [11]:

    ("precursor q <= 1%, library (inherited)", lambda d: d["Lib.Q.Value"] <= 0.01),
    ("protein group: rule D", rule_d),
])

print(f"Shared (non-proteotypic) precursor rows kept and flagged: {(filt['Proteotypic'] == 0).mean():.1%}")

6. Identification depth per run¶

Question: do any runs identify markedly fewer precursors than the rest, and does depth erode over the sequence?

Flag rule (fixed in advance): a robust z-score below −3 on precursors per run. A robust z uses the median and the MAD (median absolute deviation) instead of the mean and SD, so the outliers being hunted cannot inflate the yardstick.

In [12]:
ids = qc.ids_per_run(filt).join(meta)
ids["z_precursors"] = qc.robust_z(ids["precursors"])
ids["z_protein_groups"] = qc.robust_z(ids["protein_groups"])

from scipy.stats import spearmanr
for stype in SAMPLE_ORDER:
    sub = ids[ids["sample_type"] == stype]
    rho, p = spearmanr(sub["injection_order"], sub["precursors"])
    print(f"{LABELS[stype]:>9}: median {sub['precursors'].median():.0f} precursors "
          f"(CV {sub['precursors'].std() / sub['precursors'].mean():.1%}); "
          f"Spearman rho vs injection order = {rho:+.2f} (p = {p:.1g})")

# Size of the trend on the pooled QC: a straight-line fit, expressed per 100 injections
qc_ids = ids[ids["sample_type"] == "tQC"]
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(qc_ids["injection_order"], qc_ids["precursors"], 1)
print(f"\nPooled QC trend: {slope * 100:+.0f} precursors per 100 injections "
      f"({slope * 100 / qc_ids['precursors'].mean():+.1%} of the mean)")

print(f"Runs flagged (robust z < -3): {(ids['z_precursors'] < -3).sum()}")
ids.loc[ids["z_precursors"] < -3, ["label", "injection_order", "precursors", "z_precursors"]]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), sharex=True)
for ax, col, title in [(axes[0], "precursors", "Precursors per run"),
                       (axes[1], "protein_groups", "Protein groups per run")]:
    plotting.scatter_by_type(ax, ids["injection_order"].to_numpy(), ids[col].to_numpy(), ids["sample_type"])
    med = ids[col].median()
    mad_sd = (ids[col] - med).abs().median() * qc.MAD_TO_SD
    ax.axhline(med - 3 * mad_sd, color=FLAG, lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.text(ids["injection_order"].max(), med - 3 * mad_sd, " flag: robust z < -3",
            color=INK_MUTED, va="bottom", ha="right", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("injection order")
axes[0].set_ylabel("count")
axes[1].legend(loc="lower left")
fig.suptitle("Identification depth varies by only ~2% between runs, but erodes slowly with injection order",
             x=0.01, ha="left", fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
plotting.save_figure(fig, "01_identification_depth", FIGURES)
plt.show()

Interpretation

  • No run fails the depth flag. Within each sample type, precursor counts vary by only 1.6–2.4% (CV).
  • Plasma identifies about 120 more precursors than serum or the pooled QC (3,082 vs about 2,970). That is expected: plasma keeps fibrinogen and clotting-factor peptides that serum loses.
  • Depth erodes steadily with injection order in all three groups. The pooled QC loses about 35 precursors per 100 injections (−1.2% of its mean). No single run is an outlier, yet the trend is unmistakable: a per-run threshold misses slow decline, which is why trends are checked too.
  • Decision: keep all runs. The erosion is a first sign of sensitivity loss (§9), and it means late runs will carry more missing values. That is one more reason not to treat missingness as random.

7. Missing values: how many, and why¶

Question: are values missing because the peptide fell below the detection limit, or at random?

The answer decides imputation, if any, in Notebook 02:

  • Below detection (missing not at random, MNAR): missingness rises steeply at low intensity. Low-value imputation is defensible.
  • Random (missing completely at random, MCAR): missingness is flat across intensity. Low-value imputation would bias results downward.
In [14]:
m_prec = qc.to_matrix(filt, value="Precursor.Quantity")   # precursors x runs, raw quantities
completeness = m_prec.notna().mean(axis=1)
print(f"Matrix: {m_prec.shape[0]:,} precursors x {m_prec.shape[1]} runs; "
      f"{m_prec.isna().mean().mean():.1%} of cells missing")
print(f"Precursors quantified in every run: {(completeness == 1).mean():.1%}; "
      f"in >= 70% of runs: {(completeness >= 0.7).mean():.1%}")

miss = qc.missingness_by_intensity(m_prec, n_bins=10)
miss

Interpretation

  • 18% of matrix cells are missing, but 48% of precursors are quantified in every run and 75% in at least 70% of runs.
  • Missingness has two parts:
    • Detection limit: in the lowest-intensity decile, half the values are missing, falling to about 9% by the middle decile. That is the MNAR signature.
    • A floor of about 10% that does not shrink at high intensity. Bright precursors are not falling below detection; they miss the per-run 1% FDR cut, or lose a protein-group call, in some runs. That part behaves more like random missingness.
  • Implication for Notebook 02: a single imputation rule would be wrong for one part or the other. Options:
    • a mixed strategy: low-value imputation only for features that are low and mostly missing, with nothing imputed for the rest
    • models that tolerate missing values without imputing
  • The choice between them will be tested there.

8. Quantitative precision¶

Question: how reproducible are the quantities, and do the plasma and serum wells hold different samples or replicates of the same material?

  • CV (coefficient of variation) = SD / mean, computed on the raw, un-normalized quantities.
  • A feature is included only if it is quantified in at least 70% of the runs of that sample type.
  • Raw quantities are the honest baseline: this is the variation normalization will have to remove.
In [16]:
m_pg = qc.to_matrix(filt, value="PG.Quantity", feature="Protein.Group")

cv_rows, cv_values = [], {}
for level, matrix in [("precursor", m_prec), ("protein group", m_pg)]:
    for stype in SAMPLE_ORDER:
        runs = meta.index[meta["sample_type"] == stype]
        cv = qc.cv_percent(matrix[runs], min_fraction=0.7)
        cv_values[(level, stype)] = cv
        cv_rows.append({"level": level, "sample type": LABELS[stype], "features": len(cv),
                        "median CV %": cv.median(), "% features with CV < 20%": (cv < 20).mean() * 100})
cv_table = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows).set_index(["level", "sample type"]).round(1)
cv_table

# Are plasma wells different people, or one material? Proteins whose levels differ
# several-fold between individuals (Lp(a), haptoglobin) would show CVs far above
# the pooled-QC CV if each well held a different donor.
inter_individual = {"LPA": "lipoprotein(a)", "HP": "haptoglobin", "APOA2": "apolipoprotein A-II",
                    "HPX": "hemopexin", "IGHM": "IgM heavy chain"}

for gene, name in inter_individual.items():

    if len(pgs) == 0:
        continue
    row = {"protein": f"{gene} ({name})"}
    for stype in SAMPLE_ORDER:
        vals = m_pg.loc[pgs[0], meta.index[meta["sample_type"] == stype]].dropna()
        row[f"CV % {LABELS[stype]}"] = vals.std() / vals.mean() * 100
    rows.append(row)
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("protein").round(0)

Interpretation

  • Raw CVs are about 21–25% in every group, and only 23–47% of features fall below 20%.
  • The pooled QC over its first 10 injections has a median CV of 7.1%. Over all 39 injections it is 20.6%. So short-term precision is good, and roughly two-thirds of the long-run variance comes from drift across the sequence (§9), not from injection-to-injection noise. Normalization should recover most of it.
  • The plasma and serum wells are technical replicates, not different people. Lp(a) and haptoglobin differ several-fold to tenfold between individuals, yet their CVs across plasma wells (23–25%) match the pooled QC. Each matrix is therefore one commercial material pipetted into many wells. This is a precision experiment, so:
    • every within-matrix difference is technical
    • plasma vs serum is a matrix difference with technical n, which must not be read as biology
  • The STAR Methods agree (pooled-donor plasma, pooled commercial serum). The data established this first; the methods confirm it rather than being the basis for it.
  • Mixed lots would show up here. The methods list two products per matrix. If wells mixed two lots, proteins that differ between the lots would show CVs well above the QC. None of the inter-individual proteins do.
  • This gives Notebook 02 a clean objective. A good normalization should shrink within-matrix CVs towards the 7% short-term level while keeping the plasma–serum fibrinogen difference (§12).

9. Signal drift across the run¶

Question: does MS signal change with injection order?

  • Metric: median log2 quantity per run, computed over the precursors quantified in every run.
  • Why a fixed precursor set: if a run loses its weakest precursors, a median over "whatever was found" rises, which hides a loss of sensitivity.
  • Why raw quantities: DIA-NN's normalised quantities are designed to remove exactly this trend, so they would conceal the drift we want to measure.
In [20]:
signal, n_shared = qc.median_log2_signal(m_prec)
drift = meta.join(signal.rename("median_log2"))
print(f"Precursors quantified in all {m_prec.shape[1]} runs: {n_shared:,}")

for stype in SAMPLE_ORDER:
    sub = drift[drift["sample_type"] == stype]
    rho, p = spearmanr(sub["injection_order"], sub["median_log2"])
    print(f"{LABELS[stype]:>9}: Spearman rho = {rho:+.2f} (p = {p:.1g})")

qc_drift = drift[drift["sample_type"] == "tQC"]
change = qc_drift["median_log2"].iloc[-3:].mean() - qc_drift["median_log2"].iloc[:3].mean()
print(f"\nPooled QC, last 3 vs first 3 injections: {change:+.2f} log2 "
      f"= {2 ** change - 1:+.0%} change in signal")

# Largest single step between consecutive QC injections, compared with the typical step
steps = qc_drift["median_log2"].diff()
i = steps.abs().idxmax()
print(f"Largest QC-to-QC step: {steps[i]:+.2f} log2, between injections "
      f"{qc_drift['injection_order'].shift(1)[i]} and {qc_drift.loc[i, 'injection_order']} "
      f"(median absolute step {steps.abs().median():.2f})")

   Plasma: Spearman rho = -0.90 (p = 2e-34)
    Serum: Spearman rho = -0.85 (p = 2e-23)
Pooled QC: Spearman rho = -0.98 (p = 8e-29)

Pooled QC, last 3 vs first 3 injections: -0.76 log2 = -41% change in signal

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
plotting.scatter_by_type(ax, drift["injection_order"].to_numpy(), drift["median_log2"].to_numpy(),
                         drift["sample_type"], size=16, alpha=0.6)
for stype in SAMPLE_ORDER:
    sub = drift[drift["sample_type"] == stype]
    x, y = qc.lowess_trend(sub["injection_order"], sub["median_log2"], frac=0.4)
    ax.plot(x, y, color=SAMPLE_COLORS[stype], lw=2)
ax.set_xlabel("injection order")
ax.set_ylabel("median log2 quantity\n(precursors in all runs)")
ax.set_title("Signal falls steadily across the sequence, with a step near injection 200")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
plotting.save_figure(fig, "01_signal_drift", FIGURES)
plt.show()

Interpretation

  • Signal falls monotonically in every group (Spearman ρ = −0.85 to −0.98). The pooled QC loses 41% of its signal (−0.76 log2) between the first and last injections. Because plates were interleaved (§3), this is instrument drift, not a plate effect.
  • One clear step: between QC injections 195 and 206, signal drops 0.23 log2 in a single interval, about 10x the typical QC-to-QC change (0.02). Something happened on the instrument there: source cleaning, recalibration, a column change or spray instability. The file cannot say which. Check the paper's methods or ask the authors.
  • This trend is also the strongest independent evidence that N really is injection order: a random label could not produce a smooth decline in all three groups.
  • Two questions decide how Notebook 02 should correct this drift. Both are tested next:
    1. Is the drift the same for every precursor? If yes, one scale factor per run is enough.
    2. Is it linear in injection order? If yes, the authors' straight-line correction is adequate.

9b. Is the drift the same for every precursor, and is it linear?¶

  • Per-precursor fit: for each precursor quantified in at least 30 of the 39 pooled-QC runs, fit log2 quantity against injection order with a straight line.
  • Is the spread of slopes real? Estimate the slopes twice, from alternating QC injections (odd vs even). If the spread were noise, the two estimates would not agree.
  • Is a straight line enough? Add a step at injection 200 (where §9 saw the jump) and test with a nested-model F-test whether it improves the fit significantly.
  • Thresholds: α = 0.01, matching the authors' own threshold for applying a correction, so the two approaches are judged on the same footing.
In [22]:
qc_order = meta[meta["sample_type"] == "tQC"].sort_values("injection_order")
qc_log2 = np.log2(m_prec[qc_order.index])
trend = qc.per_feature_drift(qc_log2, qc_order["injection_order"], min_values=30, step_at=200)
print(f"Precursors tested: {len(trend):,}")
print(f"Significant linear drift (p < 0.01): {(trend['p_slope'] < 0.01).mean():.1%}")
print(f"Step at injection 200 improves on the straight line (p < 0.01): {(trend['p_step'] < 0.01).mean():.1%}")
lo, mid, hi = np.percentile(trend["slope"] * 100, [10, 50, 90])
print(f"Slope, log2 per 100 injections: median {mid:.2f} (10th-90th percentile {lo:.2f} to {hi:.2f})")

# Is the spread of slopes real? Estimate them twice, from alternating QC injections.
half_a = qc.per_feature_drift(qc_log2.iloc[:, 0::2], qc_order["injection_order"].iloc[0::2], min_values=15)
half_b = qc.per_feature_drift(qc_log2.iloc[:, 1::2], qc_order["injection_order"].iloc[1::2], min_values=15)
both = half_a.join(half_b, lsuffix="_a", rsuffix="_b", how="inner")
print(f"Split-half agreement of slopes: Pearson r = {np.corrcoef(both['slope_a'], both['slope_b'])[0, 1]:.2f} "
      f"({len(both):,} precursors)")

# What predicts a precursor's drift? Retention time and intensity.
trend["median_rt_min"] = filt.groupby("Precursor.Id")["RT"].median().reindex(trend.index)
trend["mean_log2"] = qc_log2.loc[trend.index].mean(axis=1)
for col, name in [("median_rt_min", "retention time"), ("mean_log2", "intensity")]:
    rho, p = spearmanr(trend["slope"], trend[col])
    p_text = "< 1e-15" if p < 1e-15 else f"= {p:.1g}"   # floating point cannot represent smaller p
    print(f"Slope vs {name}: Spearman rho = {rho:+.2f} (p {p_text})")

Precursors tested: 2,768
Significant linear drift (p < 0.01): 97.2%
Step at injection 200 improves on the straight line (p < 0.01): 60.3%
Slope, log2 per 100 injections: median -0.23 (10th-90th percentile -0.38 to -0.13)

Split-half agreement of slopes: Pearson r = 0.93 (2,724 precursors)
Slope vs retention time: Spearman rho = -0.74 (p < 1e-15)
Slope vs intensity: Spearman rho = -0.09 (p = 9e-07)

             x=0.01, ha="left", fontweight="bold")

plt.show()

Interpretation

  • Nearly every precursor drifts (about 97% have a significant slope), so there is no stable subset to anchor a correction on.
  • The drift rate is a property of each precursor, not noise. Slopes span about 3-fold (10th–90th percentile), and the two half-samples agree closely (r ≈ 0.93).
  • Retention time predicts it strongly (ρ ≈ −0.74): late-eluting, more hydrophobic peptides lose signal fastest. Intensity barely matters. This is the expected signature of progressive contamination of the column or ion source over hundreds of high-load serum injections.
  • The decline is not linear in time. For about 60% of precursors, a step at injection 200 fits significantly better than the straight line alone, and the pooled-QC residual from a straight line is a sawtooth: it rises within each half (the real decline is shallower than the line), then drops sharply at injection ~200. That is two gentler declines separated by a step, not one steady loss.

What this means for Notebook 02, and how it relates to the authors' choices

Option Verdict from this data
One global scale factor per run (median or total normalization) Insufficient. It cannot remove drift that depends on retention time.
RT-dependent normalization (what DIA-NN applied) Addresses the RT dependence, but anchors on sample medians, not on the QC.
Per-precursor straight-line correction against injection order (the authors' choice) Right idea, since drift is precursor-specific, but the wrong shape. It will leave the step and the within-segment error uncorrected.
Per-precursor or RT-binned non-linear correction anchored on the QC (LOWESS, or a running median, or the line split at the step) The candidate this data supports. The cost: the QC is a serum pool, so plasma-only precursors have no QC anchor.

Notebook 02 compares these options against the objectives set here: within-matrix CV, the drift component of the PCA, and the fibrinogen control. The analysis does not simply adopt one.

10. Retention-time stability¶

Question: does chromatography shift between runs, and does DIA-NN's per-run RT calibration absorb the shift?

  • RT shift of a run: the median, over its precursors, of (RT in this run − median RT of that precursor across all runs).
  • IQR of those deviations: the spread within the run. It tells a rigid shift (the whole run moves together, as from an LC delay) from a distortion (the gradient changed shape).
  • RT − Predicted.RT: the residual of DIA-NN's per-run calibration. If it stays small in shifted runs, the shift is absorbed.
In [24]:
rt = qc.rt_shift_per_run(filt).join(meta).join(ids[["precursors"]])
rt["calibration_residual_sd_s"] = ((filt["RT"] - filt["Predicted.RT"]) * 60).groupby(
    filt["run"].astype(str)).std()

shifted = rt[rt["rt_shift_s"].abs() > 5]
print(f"Runs shifted by more than 5 s: {len(shifted)} of {len(rt)} "
      f"(max {rt['rt_shift_s'].max():.0f} s)")
print(f"Within-run IQR of deviations, shifted runs: median {shifted['rt_dev_iqr_s'].median():.2f} s")
print(f"DIA-NN calibration residual SD: all runs {rt['calibration_residual_sd_s'].median():.2f} s, "
      f"shifted runs {shifted['calibration_residual_sd_s'].median():.2f} s")
print(f"Median precursors: shifted runs {shifted['precursors'].median():.0f}, "
      f"other runs {rt.drop(shifted.index)['precursors'].median():.0f}")

Within-run IQR of deviations, shifted runs: median 0.73 s
DIA-NN calibration residual SD: all runs 0.51 s, shifted runs 0.51 s
Median precursors: shifted runs 3025, other runs 3009

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [2, 1]})
plotting.scatter_by_type(axes[0], rt["injection_order"].to_numpy(), rt["rt_shift_s"].to_numpy(),
                         rt["sample_type"], size=18)
axes[0].set_xlabel("injection order")
axes[0].set_ylabel("RT shift vs experiment (s)")
axes[0].set_title("A minority of runs elute up to ~45 s late")
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left")

                         rt["sample_type"], size=18)
axes[1].set_xlabel("RT shift (s)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("precursors identified")

plt.show()

Interpretation

  • 21 runs are shifted by more than 5 s, up to 44 s, at random positions in the sequence. On a ~5-minute gradient, 44 s is large.
  • The shifts are rigid: within a shifted run, precursors deviate from their shift by a median IQR of only 0.73 s. The whole run moved together, which points to an LC delay (injection or valve timing), not a change in gradient shape.
  • DIA-NN's per-run calibration absorbed them completely. The residual SD is 0.51 s in shifted runs and in all runs, and shifted runs identify as many precursors as the rest (3,025 vs 3,009).
  • Decision: keep these runs. rt_shift is carried as an informational flag only. In a lab setting, though, a pattern like this would go back to the LC team, because a search with narrower RT windows, or a targeted assay, would not be as forgiving.

11. What drives variation between runs?¶

Question: before any normalization, is the dominant structure the sample matrix (plasma vs serum) or the technical drift?

  • Method: PCA on log2 protein-group quantities, using protein groups quantified in every run (no imputation yet).
  • Colouring: each plot is coloured twice, by sample type and by injection order.
  • What to look for: whichever colouring lines up with PC1 is the largest source of variance.

First, a check on the protein-level quantity itself.

  • §§8, 11 and 12 use the report's PG.Quantity.
  • The STAR Methods say the authors did not analyse that value: they computed MaxLFQ protein quantities from the filtered precursors, outside DIA-NN.
  • Before relying on PG.Quantity, then, test whether it can be reproduced from the precursor rows we actually have.
In [26]:
pg_check = filt.groupby(["run", "Protein.Group"], observed=True).agg(
    pg_quantity=("PG.Quantity", "first"), summed_precursors=("Precursor.Quantity", "sum"))
ratio = pg_check["pg_quantity"] / pg_check["summed_precursors"]
print("PG.Quantity / sum of retained precursor quantities, per protein group per run:")
print(ratio.describe(percentiles=[0.05, 0.5, 0.95]).round(2).to_string())

PG.Quantity / sum of retained precursor quantities, per protein group per run:
count    37592.00
mean         0.64
std          3.31
min          0.03
5%           0.09
50%          0.40
95%          1.00
max        511.59
  • The ratio is far from constant: median 0.40, 90% of values between 0.09 and 1.0, with extreme outliers above 100. So PG.Quantity is not any simple roll-up of the filtered precursors. It is DIA-NN's internal estimate, made before the report was filtered, and it partly reflects precursors that no longer appear in the table.
  • For QC structure, it is acceptable as a provisional summary: PCA, correlation, CV and the positive control only need a consistent per-protein value.
  • It is not acceptable as the final protein quantity. Notebook 02 builds protein quantities from the filtered precursors with a documented roll-up, and re-tests these protein-level results on them.

Pearson r between runs (log2, 165 protein groups): min 0.893, median 0.962

Interpretation

  • Two components dominate:
    • PC1 (40%) separates plasma from serum and QC, weakly tied to run order (ρ = −0.22).
    • PC2 (34%) is almost entirely injection order (ρ = −0.91). It splits into two clouds, early and late, with the gap at the signal step near injection 200 (§9).
    • Before normalization, technical drift therefore accounts for almost as much variance as the plasma/serum matrix difference.
  • The correlation heatmap agrees: every pair of runs correlates at r ≥ 0.89 (median 0.96). Plasma forms its own block, and serum and the pooled QC are nearly indistinguishable, as expected for a serum pool.
  • Implication for Notebook 02: this gives a concrete success criterion. After normalization:
    • the drift component should largely disappear
    • the matrix component should remain
  • Note that the PCA uses only the 165 protein groups quantified in all runs; how imputation changes the picture is part of Notebook 02.

12. Positive control: can the data see a difference we know is real?¶

When blood clots to make serum, fibrinogen is converted to fibrin and removed. So fibrinogen chains must be far higher in plasma than in serum, while proteins untouched by clotting (albumin, apolipoprotein A-I) should not change.

This tests the whole chain: identification, protein grouping and quantification. If the data fails it, nothing downstream can be trusted.

In [30]:

                 "serum runs quantified": int(vals[meta["sample_type"] == "Serum"].notna().sum())})
    long.append(pd.DataFrame({"gene": gene, "log2": vals, "sample_type": meta["sample_type"]}))
positive_control = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("gene").round(2)
positive_control

Interpretation

  • The positive control passes clearly. FGA, FGB and FGG are 2^4.1 to 2^8.3 times (about 16x to 300x) higher in plasma than in serum. Albumin and ApoA-I sit within ±0.15 log2 of no change.
  • The FGB and FGG fold changes are probably underestimates. FGB is quantified in only 27 of 79 serum runs, and only the serum runs with the most residual fibrinogen are detected at all. The serum median is therefore biased upward and the true difference is larger still. Notebook 02's imputation choices will move this number, which makes it a useful test of them.
  • Serum FGA values fall in two clusters (about log2 9.8 and 8.3). The same split appears in the pooled QC, which is a single pool, so it is not two commercial lots. It is not explained by injection time or by which FGA precursors were detected either. That points at PG.Quantity itself (see §11) and is one more reason to rebuild protein quantities from precursors in Notebook 02.
  • The pooled QC matches serum (log2 QC/serum ≈ 0 for every fibrinogen chain). That confirms the QC is a serum pool, as the PRIDE record states. Consequence: the QC tracks serum-matrix precision. Plasma-specific proteins such as fibrinogen are barely present in it, so the QC cannot anchor drift correction for them.

13. QC verdict per run, and what is carried forward¶

Flags are fixed rules, applied to every run the same way:

Flag Rule Type
low_ids robust z of precursors per run < −3 hard
low_correlation r to its sample type's median profile is below (median − 3 robust SD) hard
signal_outlier residual from the sample type's drift trend has robust z < −3 (a run weaker than its neighbours, not merely late in the sequence) hard
rt_shift absolute RT shift > 30 s informational only (§10 showed it costs nothing)

Exclusion rule: a run is excluded only if it fails two or more hard flags. A single marginal flag is noted, not acted on.

In [32]:
verdict = meta.join(ids[["precursors", "protein_groups", "z_precursors"]]).join(rt[["rt_shift_s"]])
verdict = verdict.join(drift[["median_log2"]])

# correlation to own sample type's median profile (log2 precursors in all runs)
verdict["r_to_reference"] = qc.correlation_to_reference(np.log2(m_prec), meta)
r = verdict["r_to_reference"]
r_cut = r.median() - 3 * (r - r.median()).abs().median() * qc.MAD_TO_SD

# signal residual after removing each sample type's own drift trend
residual = pd.Series(index=verdict.index, dtype=float)
for stype, sub in verdict.groupby("sample_type"):
    fit = np.interp(sub["injection_order"], *qc.lowess_trend(sub["injection_order"], sub["median_log2"], frac=0.4))
    residual[sub.index] = sub["median_log2"] - fit
verdict["signal_residual"] = residual

verdict["low_ids"] = verdict["z_precursors"] < -3
verdict["low_correlation"] = verdict["r_to_reference"] < r_cut
verdict["signal_outlier"] = qc.robust_z(verdict["signal_residual"]) < -3
verdict["rt_shift"] = verdict["rt_shift_s"].abs() > 30
hard = ["low_ids", "low_correlation", "signal_outlier"]
verdict["n_hard_flags"] = verdict[hard].sum(axis=1)
verdict["exclude"] = verdict["n_hard_flags"] >= 2

print(f"Correlation cut-off: r < {r_cut:.4f}")
print(verdict[hard + ["rt_shift", "exclude"]].sum().to_string())
flagged = verdict[verdict[hard + ["rt_shift"]].any(axis=1)]
flagged[["label", "injection_order", "precursors", "r_to_reference", "signal_residual"] + hard + ["rt_shift", "exclude"]]

# Median residual for each plate row, and a test of the two rows that stand out
plates_only = verdict[verdict["sample_type"] != "tQC"]
display(plates_only.pivot_table(index="plate", columns="well_row", values="signal_residual",
                                aggfunc="median").round(2))

from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu
for row, stype in [("H", "Serum"), ("F", "Plasma")]:
    in_row = plates_only[(plates_only["plate"] == "3") & (plates_only["well_row"] == row)]
    rest = plates_only[(plates_only["sample_type"] == stype) & ~plates_only.index.isin(in_row.index)]
    _, p = mannwhitneyu(in_row["signal_residual"], rest["signal_residual"])
    print(f"Plate 3 row {row} ({stype}, n={len(in_row)}): median residual {in_row['signal_residual'].median():+.2f} "
          f"vs {rest['signal_residual'].median():+.2f} for other {stype.lower()} wells (Mann-Whitney p = {p:.1g})")

# Carry the plate-row median forward so Notebook 02 can test whether normalization removes it
verdict["plate_row_median_residual"] = verdict.groupby(["plate", "well_row"])["signal_residual"].transform("median")

Plate 3 row H (Serum, n=11): median residual -0.36 vs -0.01 for other serum wells (Mann-Whitney p = 4e-06)
Plate 3 row F (Plasma, n=12): median residual -0.19 vs +0.01 for other plasma wells (Mann-Whitney p = 4e-05)

Interpretation

  • Every excluded run is a serum well in plate 3, row H. The whole row is weak: median −0.36 log2, about 22% less signal than the drift trend, with lower correlation and about 130 fewer precursors than other serum wells (Mann–Whitney p ≈ 4×10⁻⁶).
  • Plate 3, row F (plasma) is weaker too, though less so (−0.19 log2).
  • On the same plate, rows B and D run slightly high (+0.08 to +0.09 log2). So plate 3 has a top-to-bottom gradient, which no other plate shows.
  • These wells were injected at random points across the sequence (positions 28 to 385). The cause therefore sat in the plate, not in the instrument at a particular time. A gradient down one plate is typical of a preparation step that acted unevenly across it: uneven heating or evaporation during digestion, or a multichannel liquid handler dispensing unevenly down the plate. Which one cannot be told from the data.
  • The exclusion rule was fixed before looking, and it is applied as written: 4 runs are excluded and the other row-H wells are kept. Tightening the rule now that the pattern is visible would be choosing thresholds to fit the data.
  • What we do instead: carry plate_row_median_residual forward. Notebook 02 then tests whether normalization rescues these wells:
    • If the problem is less material loaded, per-run scaling fixes it.
    • If the low correlation reflects a real composition change (incomplete digestion, for example), it will not.

Summary¶

Area Finding Carried into Notebook 02
Provenance Commercial control runs from Messner et al. 2020 (PXD018874), interleaved with Generation Scotland serum samples (not deposited). DIA-NN 1.7.10, library refined on the experiment. Filters q 0.01 / library q 0.005 / PG q 0.05, confirmed by the STAR Methods. Upstream choices and our response are listed in §1.
Protein quantity The report's PG.Quantity cannot be rebuilt from the filtered precursors. Notebook 02 rolls up proteins from precursors and re-tests protein-level results.
Design Plasma and serum wells are technical replicates of one material each (inter-individual proteins show QC-level CVs). Plates were interleaved across the run. Within-matrix variance is purely technical: the objective for normalization.
Identification filter Rule D: PG q ≤ 1% in ≥25% of runs of one matrix. Keeps 184 protein groups (180 per run) and fibrinogen; loses VWF and F5, which are marginal in a 5-minute gradient. Sensitivity check under rules B and E.
Depth Stable (CV ≈ 2%), no outliers, slow erosion of about 1% per 100 injections. Late runs carry more missing values.
Missingness 18% of cells. A detection-limit component at low intensity plus a ~10% floor at all intensities. Mixed imputation strategy, or none.
Precision Raw CV about 21–25%. Short-term QC CV 7%, so most of the variance is drift. Target: within-matrix CV close to 7%.
Drift −41% signal over the run, a step near injection 200, the same in all groups. Drift is precursor-specific (split-half r ≈ 0.93), strongly RT-dependent (ρ ≈ −0.74) and non-linear (a step term is significant for ~60% of precursors). Global scaling is insufficient and the authors' straight-line correction is the wrong shape. Compare RT-aware and non-linear QC-anchored corrections.
Retention time 21 rigid shifts up to 44 s, fully absorbed by DIA-NN calibration. Informational flag only.
Structure PC1 = matrix (40%), PC2 = drift (34%). Success = drift component removed, matrix component kept.
Positive control Fibrinogen 16–300x higher in plasma than serum; albumin and ApoA-I flat. The QC is a serum pool. Use as a fixed truth when comparing normalization and imputation.
Run QC 4 runs excluded (all plate 3, row H serum). A plate-row sample-prep effect in plate 3, rows H and F. Test whether normalization rescues the remaining plate-3 wells.

Limitations

  • No access to the raw search: the library, its refinement and the protein inference are inherited. The library was refined using runs (the GS samples) that we cannot see.
  • The protein-group rule approximates a global FDR rather than estimating one.
  • The cause of the step near injection 200 is unknown.
  • The cause of the plate-3 effect is inferred, not confirmed.
